\!git clone https://github.com/boa-collaboration/boa-constrictor.git  
%cd boa-constrictor

And downloaded the requirements.txt in the environment.

While reading the code I came across the concept of a streaming state cache. At first I described this loosely as "stream referencing" but after going back to the paper I understood it more precisely. The streaming state is the recurrent hidden state h(t) that acts as a compressed representation of the entire history of input bytes processed so far. This means the model does not need to re-process the entire byte sequence for every new byte it encounters — instead it just updates h(t) with the new byte and moves forward. This is what makes autoregressive compression feasible on long sequences without exploding memory usage. The `tag_mamba_layers_with_ids` function in model.py is responsible for assigning unique IDs to each Mamba layer, and `bump_offset` updates the position counter in the inference cache so the model always knows where it is in the stream.

I ran into an error while downloading requirements.txt:

× Building wheel for causal-conv1d (pyproject.toml) did not run successfully.  
× Building wheel for mamba-ssm (pyproject.toml) did not run successfully.  
Failed to build causal-conv1d mamba-ssm

From what I could see, this was an error related to building the environment in Colab. I googled for a quick solution and it turned out to be a CUDA version mismatch. I copied these commands to check:

\!nvcc \--version  
\!python \-c "import torch; print(torch.\_\_version\_\_); print(torch.cuda.is\_available())"

Output:

Cuda compilation tools, release 12.8, V12.8.93  
2.10.0+cu128  
True

So Colab provides CUDA 12.8 and PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128. I asked Gemini for possible solutions. It suggested 3 options, but none of them worked — each led to a new error.

After more research, I found an article on LinkedIn that helped me understand what was actually going on. Here is what I learned:

mamba-ssm contains C++/CUDA code that must be compiled during installation. For this to succeed, three things must match:

1. CUDA Toolkit (nvcc) version  
2. PyTorch CUDA version  
3. causal-conv1d/mamba-ssm build system

When I tried installing requirements.txt directly, the requirements wanted PyTorch cu130 but Colab had CUDA 12.8 — a mismatch. When I forced PyTorch to cu130, it changed correctly but nvcc was still 12.8, with different compiler internals — failure again.

The real fix was to find which CUDA version Colab's actual compiler defaults to (12.1) and match PyTorch to that:

python  
\# 1\. Install correct PyTorch for Colab's actual compiler  
\!pip install torch==2.4.0 \--index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121

\# 2\. Uninstall any broken installs  
\!pip uninstall \-y mamba-ssm causal-conv1d

\# 3\. Install Mamba using the PyTorch we just installed  
\!pip install causal-conv1d mamba-ssm \--no-build-isolation  
\`\`\`

By installing PyTorch cu121, I matched the real underlying toolkit. causal-conv1d compiled successfully after that.

I am now ready to explore which approach to use to replace MambaBlock.

Mar 10:

Started by reading model.py line by line and used Qwen 3.5 to explain each section and clarify what each part does.

The first part configures whether CUDA is available, which determines which version of Mamba to use. \`tag\_mamba\_layers\_with\_ids(model)\` loops through every layer in the model, finds the Mamba layers, and assigns each a unique ID. \`bump\_offset\` updates the position counter in the inference cache , in other words the model always knows where it is when processing the stream.

After going through the entire code, I started thinking about which backbone to use as a replacement.

Backbone selection:

From my understanding of the BOA paper, the main reason Mamba was chosen over Transformers is to avoid O(N²) complexity, This made me think GRU or LSTM were the natural alternatives since both have linear O(L) complexity.

I presumed GRU was still the right choice for this exercise because:  
\- Single hidden state maps cleanly onto BOA's existing streaming cache interface  
\- No custom CUDA kernels required — which directly addresses the portability problem the paper identifies  
\- Standard PyTorch implementation, deployable anywhere

I implemented \`model\_gru.py\` with \`GRUBlock\` as a drop-in replacement for \`MambaBlock\`. Main design decisions:

\- \`nn.GRU\` with \`batch\_first=True\` so input shape \`\[B, L, D\]\` matches BOA's pipeline  
\- Same \`LayerNorm → sequence model → LayerNorm → feedforward\` structure as MambaBlock  
\- Same residual connection \`x \+ y\` to stabilize training  
\- \`forward()\` accepts \`inference\_params=None\` for interface compatibility  
\- \`step()\` processes single tokens with GRU hidden state passed through, enabling streaming

Sanity check confirmed:  
\`\`\`  
Output shape: torch.Size(\[1, 64, 256\])  
Parameters: 3,882,496  
\`\`\`

Shape \`\[1, 64, 256\]\` — batch=1, sequence=64 bytes, 256 possible next-byte predictions — identical interface to the original.

\*\*Running the experiment:\*\*

Dataset: \`CMS\_DATA\_float32.bin\` — 47.61 MB of real CMS detector data from the LHC.

One more missing dependency appeared — \`pybind11\`, required to build the GPU range coder CUDA extension. Installed separately:  
\`\`\`  
\!pip install pybind11==3.0.1  
\`\`\`

Then a cuDNN version conflict appeared:  
\`\`\`  
RuntimeError: cuDNN version incompatibility: PyTorch was compiled against (9, 10, 2\)   
but found runtime version (9, 1, 0\)

This is directly related to what the paper calls the portability problem. BOA's encoder and decoder must stay in perfect lockstep; both must produce bit-identical probability distributions at every step. This is what the paper refers to as the "critical barrier to deployment." The cuDNN conflict I hit is exactly this problem in practice; a different cuDNN version would produce different floating-point results. The fix was to clear the conflicting library path and disable cuDNN:

python  
import os  
os.environ\['LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH'\] \= ''  
import torch  
torch.backends.cudnn.enabled \= False  
\`\`\`

**![][image1]**

To compare against another architecture, I implemented \`model\_lstm.py\` with the same structure but using \`nn.LSTM\`. The key difference is LSTM maintains two hidden states — cell state \`c\` and hidden state \`h\` , compared to GRU's single hidden state, giving it more expressive gating at the cost of a slightly more complex streaming cache.

**![][image2]**

**Summary:**

| Backbone | Ratio | Throughput | Parameters |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Mamba (trained, paper) | 44.14x | — | \~4.5M |
| GRU (untrained) | 1.0352x | 0.0459 MB/s | 3.88M |
| LSTM (untrained) | 1.0026x | 0.0471 MB/s | 4.41M |

The big takeaway isn't whether GRU or LSTM did better (they were basically the same, around 1.02-1.03x). What's key is that the 44x compression in the BOA paper isn't really due to Mamba; it's because the model was trained. This is basic cross-entropy: a trained model predicts bytes confidently, so the range coder gives them shorter codes, boosting compression. An untrained model is just guessing, so compression stays low.

Mamba's real advantage shows up in throughput at scale, not in this untrained baseline. The 0.0485 MB/s I got from GRU vs the paper's \~2.92 MB/s gap is partly because GRU is symbol-sequential, each hidden state h(t) must wait for h(t-1) before it can be computed, which means the GPU cannot be fully saturated. Mamba's parallel scan removes this bottleneck. At the LHC scale, processing petabytes of data, that throughput gap matters a lot.

The difficulty of installing CUDA itself demonstrated the portability problem in practice. GRU and LSTM require no custom CUDA kernels, so they are deployable on any hardware that runs standard PyTorch. As future work, I am considering running tests on other sub-quadratic architectures, such as MinGRU and Hawkk. What I'm really trying to find out is whether any of these alternatives can provide a better balance between the Compression Ratio and the Storage-Saving Rate than the standard Mamba setup.
